I reincarnated in Charleston, SC and currently live in Los Angeles, CA. A sacred rebel at heart, I believe in cooperation over competition and speaking my truth even if it ruffles a few feathers.
I reincarnated in Charleston, SC and currently live in Los Angeles, CA. A sacred rebel at heart, I believe in cooperation over competition and speaking my truth even if it ruffles a few feathers.
Apple renewed Qualcomm’s patent license while actively building custom modems to replace Qualcomm chips.
Qualcomm disclosed only the April 1, 2027 renewal date, revealing no duration, royalty rates, or financial terms.
Distinguish Qualcomm’s chip supply revenue from its patent licensing arm; this deal only protects the latter.
Apple is building its own custom silicon modem chips. Apple also just renewed its patent license with Qualcomm. Both things are true, and that tension is exactly what makes the September 24, 2026 announcement worth parsing carefully.
The renewal, effective April 1, 2027, confirms that Apple still needs access to Qualcomm’s wireless intellectual property even as it works to reduce its reliance on Qualcomm modem hardware. What it does not confirm is how much Apple will pay, how long the agreement runs, or whether the royalty economics changed at all. That silence splits the announcement into two very different stories depending on which part of Qualcomm’s business you are watching.
Qualcomm’s chip supply operation and its patent licensing arm are separate businesses, and this announcement only speaks to one of them.
Qualcomm operates two distinct revenue streams that are easy to conflate. One is its chip supply business, which sells modem hardware to device manufacturers including Apple. The other is Qualcomm Technology Licensing, known as QTL, which collects royalties from manufacturers that use Qualcomm’s cellular patents.
If you follow Qualcomm’s earnings, these two revenue streams matter very differently here. Apple renewing the patent license continues the licensing relationship, but it does not shield Qualcomm’s modem chip revenue.
According to Reuters, the renewed agreement extends Qualcomm’s licensing relationship with Apple even as Apple reduces its reliance on Qualcomm modem chips. MacRumors reported separately that Apple’s transition toward custom-designed modems is ongoing, though that reporting represents secondary coverage rather than an official Apple product disclosure.
The practical implication: Apple could reduce or phase down its Qualcomm modem purchases while remaining subject to a patent license. Whether it will, and at what rate, is a question this announcement does not answer.
Qualcomm confirmed a renewal date and nothing else.
The renewed agreement takes effect April 1, 2027. Qualcomm disclosed neither its duration nor its financial terms, according to the company’s official press release on PR Newswire and reporting from Yahoo Finance.
John Han, Qualcomm’s executive vice president and general manager of Qualcomm Technology Licensing, offered a single-sentence response in the company’s release: “We are pleased to extend the Apple license agreement.” The brevity of that statement is not incidental. It reflects exactly how much either company chose to reveal, which limits any precise forecast of what the renewal means for Qualcomm’s earnings.
The announcement confirms a future licensing relationship between the two companies. It does not establish whether Qualcomm negotiated favorable terms, unfavorable ones, or something in between.
This is actually the second time these companies have found their way back to the table after a serious fight.
Qualcomm and Apple settled years of worldwide litigation in 2019. That settlement produced a six-year global patent-license agreement beginning April 1, 2019, along with a separate multiyear modem-supply arrangement, according to Reuters. The current agreement ran through March 31, 2027; the renewal follows the expiration of that existing term.
That history matters for a specific reason. The companies have already demonstrated they can fight bitterly, settle, and continue doing business. A second renewal does not guarantee harmony, but it does indicate that Qualcomm’s patent portfolio carries commercial weight with Apple.
The Unverified Numbers Behind the Bull Case
The licensing-versus-chips distinction has a logical foundation, but the financial figures attached to the bullish reading require independent confirmation.
Some analysts and investors interpret the renewal as evidence that Apple’s modem insourcing threatens Qualcomm’s chip revenue far more directly than its royalty revenue. That structural argument is defensible based on verified reporting.
Figures circulating in investor commentary were not independently verified against Qualcomm’s official filings in available sources. Those figures include specific QTL quarterly revenue and margin numbers, automotive growth rates, a reported BMW partnership, free cash flow totals, and valuation comparisons to Broadcom. Those numbers should be confirmed against Qualcomm’s Form 10-Q or official earnings release before being treated as established fact.
The specific financial case built around the structural argument requires primary-source confirmation before you treat it as settled.
Undisclosed terms are the central limitation of any optimistic reading.
Without knowing the duration or royalty rate, it is not possible to determine from this announcement whether Qualcomm preserved its prior Apple-related royalty economics or accepted less favorable conditions. Apple’s modem transition also remains a concrete threat to Qualcomm’s component revenue, independent of whatever the patent agreement says.
Any argument that automotive, IoT, or data-center growth will offset declining handset revenue depends on margin comparisons, capital requirements, and execution timelines. This announcement does not address any of those factors.
What the Renewal Resolves, and What It Does Not
The announcement answers one narrow question and leaves the more consequential ones open.
The renewal confirms that Qualcomm’s wireless patent portfolio still holds enough commercial value that Apple agreed to continue licensing it rather than walk away. That is not nothing.
What the announcement does not tell you is how long the agreement runs or what Apple agreed to pay. The term, the economics, and the pace of Apple’s modem transition all remain open. So does whether Qualcomm’s diversification efforts can deliver at the margins required to replace lost chip revenue. Those answers will come from future earnings disclosures, not from a two-sentence press release.

[News] Qualcomm Says Announced 2nm Chips Will Use TSMC, Keeps Door Open to Samsung Foundry
Samsung Foundry’s efforts to secure major customers have been closely watched, with the possibility of future cooperation with Qualcomm remaining open. According to Chosun Biz, Chris Patrick, Qualcomm senior vice president and general manager of mobile handsets, said the company is likely to work with suppliers that offer strong technology, while emphasizing its partnerships with both Samsung Foundry and TSMC. His comments do not confirm that Qualcomm will adopt Samsung’s 2nm process, but the company has not ruled out Samsung as a foundry partner for future products.
For now, however, Patrick confirmed that all 2nm products Qualcomm has announced will be manufactured by TSMC, as the report points out.
New 2nm Snapdragon Chips Push Mobile CPU Past 5GHz
Those 2nm products are now taking shape in Qualcomm’s latest flagship mobile lineup. According to a separate Chosun Biz report, Qualcomm unveiled two new 2nm flagship mobile APs, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. Both feature Qualcomm’s next-generation in-house Oryon CPU, which uses two prime cores and six performance cores and is the first mobile CPU to exceed a maximum clock speed of 5GHz.
The higher-end platform also brings a major graphics upgrade, with its latest Adreno GPU delivering 44% higher performance than its predecessor. Qualcomm has also added dedicated AI capabilities to the GPU to improve graphics processing and efficiency.
On-device AI is another major focus of the new generation. The upgraded Hexagon NPU, combined with UFS 5.0 and intelligent flash memory management, enables MoE models with more than 30 billion parameters to run directly on smartphones, Chosun Biz notes. Qualcomm has also upgraded its Sensing Hub to process voice and surrounding context continuously at low power, supporting features such as speaker recognition and personalized AI agents.
The first devices powered by the new chips were also unveiled, with Xiaomi introducing its Xiaomi 18 Pro series. The company plans to use the two new Snapdragon platforms across different products and roll them out globally within the year, according to Chosun Biz.

Qualcomm to Acquire PickNik to Advance the Future of Open Robotics and Physical AI
Highlights:
Qualcomm to acquire PickNik Robotics, reinforcing its continued investment in driving an open ecosystem for advanced physical AI and robotics.
MoveIt, one of the most widely used open-source robotics manipulation frameworks, is expected to offer streamlined integration with Qualcomm® Dragonwing™ Robotics platforms and Arduino® platforms, expanding access to advanced robotics, and aiming to enable millions of developers to leverage edge AI and heterogeneous compute to build the next generation of intelligent robots.
Qualcomm remains committed to PickNik's open-source development, with MoveIt 1 and MoveIt 2 to remain open, community-driven, and supported across third-party hardware platforms.
Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. today announced its agreement to acquire PickNik Inc., an industry recognized robotics software company and longtime steward of MoveIt, one of the world's most widely adopted open-source robotics manipulation frameworks. This acquisition is intended to strengthen Qualcomm Technologies' commitment to fostering an open robotics ecosystem, providing developers with the tools, software, and frameworks needed to move more efficiently from research and experimentation to prototyping, deployment, and production at scale. In addition to remaining open-source, MoveIt is expected to offer streamlined integration with Dragonwing robotics platforms-providing developers with a more streamlined path from AI models such as VLAs and VLMs to planning, manipulation, and real-time control. The closing of this transaction is subject to customary closing conditions.
"Robotics is one of the most exciting frontiers of physical AI, and software is the connective tissue that turns great hardware into great robots," said Nakul Duggal, EVP and Group GM, Automotive, Industrial and Embedded IoT, and Robotics, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. "PickNik has earned tremendous trust within the global robotics community through its stewardship of MoveIt and its commitment to open-source innovation. Together, we plan to make it easier for developers to build advanced robotic applications on Dragonwing robotics platforms, while continuing to support the openness and collaboration that have made MoveIt successful."
"Since our founding, PickNik's mission has been to provide industries with a powerful, open platform that accelerates innovation and development of advanced robotics, well beyond traditional factories," said Dave Coleman, Founder and Chief Product Officer, PickNik Inc. "Joining Qualcomm Technologies will allow us to accelerate that mission, expand investment in MoveIt as a leading AI training platform for robotics, and deliver even more value to developers while preserving the openness, community collaboration, and cross-platform support that have always been central to our approach."
"MoveIt is entering an exciting new chapter with the resources and support to help expand its impact," said Dave Grant, Chief Executive Officer, PickNik Inc. "We look forward to joining Qualcomm Technologies and building on MoveIt's momentum."
Built atop the Robot Operating System (ROS), MoveIt has been used extensively by developers, students, researchers, and commercial robotics organizations worldwide to create sophisticated robotic applications in nearly every industry, including industrial automation, service robotics, mobile manipulation, and emerging physical AI systems.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik recognize that MoveIt's value comes from its openness, broad adoption, and active developer community. Accordingly, Qualcomm Technologies intends for MoveIt to remain open-source under its existing license with community-driven roadmaps and open resources. Qualcomm Technologies also intends to continue supporting MoveIt across third-party hardware providers. MoveIt's hardware-agnostic design is a key enabler of innovation, giving developers the freedom to choose the robot, compute platforms, and sensor components that best fit their needs.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik are both founding members of the Open Source Robotics Alliance (OSRA) and Qualcomm Technologies intends to continue driving major projects including Space ROS, a hardened version of ROS optimized for critical applications such as space exploration. Qualcomm Technologies will continue to support the open source development of MoveIt and ROS.
Accelerating Robotics Development on Dragonwing and Arduino
As part of the acquisition, MoveIt, MoveIt Pro - PickNik's commercial platform designed to support advanced robotics systems - and future PickNik technologies, are poised to become more closely integrated with Dragonwing robotics platforms. This integration will enable developers to more easily take advantage of Dragonwing's advanced AI, heterogeneous computing, connectivity, and real-time robotics capabilities in order to help simplify robotics development, shorten deployment timelines, and accelerate innovation across a broad range of robotic applications. Developers building on Dragonwing should benefit from first-class, optimized support for MoveIt's motion planning, manipulation, perception, and kinematics capabilities-helping to move from prototype to production faster while maintaining the flexibility to develop for diverse robotics architectures and deployment environments.
Starting with Arduino® VENTUNO™ Q boards, MoveIt integration with Arduino aims to make advanced robotics, edge AI, and heterogeneous compute more accessible than ever. This integration seeks to extend powerful motion planning and autonomy capabilities to target millions of developers, helping shorten the journey from prototype to production-ready robots.
This week at ROSCon Toronto, Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik will be displaying MoveIt Pro running on VENTUNO Q and Dragonwing robotics platforms. Visit the Qualcomm Technologies (9/10 & 16) and PickNik (7) booths to learn more.

"Since our founding, PickNik's mission has been to provide industries with a powerful, open platform that accelerates innovation and development of advanced robotics, well beyond traditional factories," said Dave Coleman, Founder and Chief Product Officer, PickNik Inc. "Joining Qualcomm Technologies will allow us to accelerate that mission, expand investment in MoveIt as a leading AI training platform for robotics, and deliver even more value to developers while preserving the openness, community collaboration, and cross-platform support that have always been central to our approach."
"MoveIt is entering an exciting new chapter with the resources and support to help expand its impact," said Dave Grant, Chief Executive Officer, PickNik Inc. "We look forward to joining Qualcomm Technologies and building on MoveIt's momentum."
Built atop the Robot Operating System (ROS), MoveIt has been used extensively by developers, students, researchers, and commercial robotics organizations worldwide to create sophisticated robotic applications in nearly every industry, including industrial automation, service robotics, mobile manipulation, and emerging physical AI systems.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik recognize that MoveIt's value comes from its openness, broad adoption, and active developer community. Accordingly, Qualcomm Technologies intends for MoveIt to remain open-source under its existing license with community-driven roadmaps and open resources. Qualcomm Technologies also intends to continue supporting MoveIt across third-party hardware providers. MoveIt's hardware-agnostic design is a key enabler of innovation, giving developers the freedom to choose the robot, compute platforms, and sensor components that best fit their needs.
Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik are both founding members of the Open Source Robotics Alliance (OSRA) and Qualcomm Technologies intends to continue driving major projects including Space ROS, a hardened version of ROS optimized for critical applications such as space exploration. Qualcomm Technologies will continue to support the open source development of MoveIt and ROS.
Accelerating Robotics Development on Dragonwing and Arduino
As part of the acquisition, MoveIt, MoveIt Pro — PickNik's commercial platform designed to support advanced robotics systems — and future PickNik technologies, are poised to become more closely integrated with Dragonwing robotics platforms. This integration will enable developers to more easily take advantage of Dragonwing's advanced AI, heterogeneous computing, connectivity, and real-time robotics capabilities in order to help simplify robotics development, shorten deployment timelines, and accelerate innovation across a broad range of robotic applications. Developers building on Dragonwing should benefit from first-class, optimized support for MoveIt's motion planning, manipulation, perception, and kinematics capabilities—helping to move from prototype to production faster while maintaining the flexibility to develop for diverse robotics architectures and deployment environments.
Starting with Arduino® VENTUNO™ Q boards, MoveIt integration with Arduino aims to make advanced robotics, edge AI, and heterogeneous compute more accessible than ever. This integration seeks to extend powerful motion planning and autonomy capabilities to target millions of developers, helping shorten the journey from prototype to production-ready robots.
This week at ROSCon Toronto, Qualcomm Technologies and PickNik will be displaying MoveIt Pro running on VENTUNO Q and Dragonwing robotics platforms. Visit the Qualcomm Technologies (9/10 & 16) and PickNik (7) booths to learn more.

Ziad Asghar, general manager of XR, Wearables and Personal AI, sits on stage debuting Qualcomm’s silicon during the Snapdragon Summit in Maui, Hawaii. (Qualcomm)
By Noelle Harff | noelle.harff@sduniontribune.com
PUBLISHED: October 1, 2026 at 2:32 PM PDT | UPDATED: October 1, 2026 at 2:46 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
Qualcomm had a lot to talk about last week.
Beyond debuting new silicon designed to run AI processing on smartphones, glasses and earbuds, the San Diego semiconductor giant ended the event on Sept. 24 with a major update: a one-line statement confirming it extended its licensing agreement with Apple starting April 1, 2027 — the same day the current agreement was set to expire.
Here is what you need to know:
Qualcomm’s chips enable Apple’s iPhones — along with Android and Samsung devices — to connect to cellular networks. The chipmaker is a leader in the space and holds a patent on the crucial tech.
In 2017, Apple attempted to reduce its dependence on Qualcomm and began developing its own modems.
Years of litigation ensued, leading analysts to assume Apple would officially sever ties with Qualcomm when the licensing patent expired on April 1, 2027.
In the time since, Apple paid $1 billion to Intel for its modem business and spent over six years building its own chip to reduce its reliance on Qualcomm.
“The question of ‘will they or won’t they’ around this issue” is answered, at least for now, said Stacy Rasgon, a semiconductor analyst for Bernstein.
Rasgon’s firm estimates the deal will generate $1.5 billion to $1.7 billion in annual revenue, or roughly $7.50 per phone. But those are estimates based on historical data, as the official press release was only one sentence.
Everyone except Qualcomm and Apple remains in the dark about specific terms, Rasgon said, noting that analysts and investors are eager to learn the duration of the deal. He expects more details during the company’s next earnings call on Nov. 4.
Qualcomm — and most tech companies today — are pushing a narrative that artificial intelligence will change everything.
And while AI has entered everyday conversations and made writing emails a bit easier, it has yet to meaningfully impact daily life for most people.
After all, who actually has an AI assistant?
During his keynote speech, Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon outlined how to get one during what he calls the “agentic age.”
We’re moving from interacting with tools to collaborating with the technology, Amon explained.
To illustrate what that means, Qualcomm demonstrated smart glasses integrated with Mastercard.
In a shopping demonstration, a user wearing smart glasses asked an AI agent integrated into the glasses to compare an in-store computer price against online deals.
The agent scanned options, found a cheaper deal online, placed the order and confirmed a delivery date.
The agent was able to see the environment, hear the user, and process the request natively on the glasses, with the help of Qualcomm’s new silicon.
“Traditional digital experiences wait for a query. Proactive agents can recognize when context and likely intent create an opportunity to help before the user begins a search,” said Sundar Subramanian, director of AI product management at Qualcomm.
Qualcomm executives described the conventional “burdens” of shopping — discovering items, evaluating purchases and checking your wallet to see if you can afford the product.
“Technology has made each step easier,” Subramanian said. But don’t worry, “the overall cognitive burden still sits largely with the user.”
Whether that sounds convenient or dystopian, these AI agents are already arriving.

Qualcomm Stock Has an Opportunity Investors May Be Underestimating
Qualcomm just posted 61% automotive growth and raised its non-handset target to $40 billion, yet the market keeps valuing it like a company living and dying by smartphone chips. Something in that gap is worth a closer look.
Published September 27, 2026, 1:00pm ET · 3 min read
Price Targets desk. Editor: Vandita Jadeja.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM | QCOM Price Prediction) is building a data center franchise that management believes can hit $15 billion in revenue by fiscal 2029. That opportunity is not fully priced in.
Our 24/7 Wall St. price target for Qualcomm is $228.68 over the next 12 months, implying 16.27% upside from $194.38. We rate the stock a buy with 90% confidence.
Qualcomm rallied 23.28% over the past month and 15.44% year to date, though it sits roughly 25% below its 52-week high of $257.56.
Fiscal Q3 2026 results showed revenue of $9.947 billion (beating estimates by 2.84%) with non-GAAP EPS of $2.21, missing consensus by 0.49%. Handsets fell 20% year over year, but automotive grew 61% to $1.588 billion, marking 23 consecutive quarters of double-digit growth.
CEO Cristiano Amon raised the long-term non-handset target to $40 billion by fiscal 2029. Two hyperscaler custom silicon programs begin shipping in the December quarter, with the first high-bandwidth compute solution launching in mid-2027.
Automotive run-rate exiting fiscal 2026 was lifted to approximately $7 billion from $6 billion. Non-handset growth is guided to accelerate from 24% in fiscal 2026 to greater than 60% in fiscal 2027. If execution holds, the bull case reaches $245.07 within 12 months.
The bear case starts with Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL). Management expects Qualcomm’s modem share in the upcoming iPhone to be materially lower than the prior 20% estimate, with Apple revenue projected to fall roughly 50% from September to December.
Add memory-driven input cost inflation, QCT gross margins slipping below the historical 48% to 50% band, and a 1.5% to 2% margin drag from initial data center ramps.
Q3 operating income fell 41.13% year over year. Bulls counter that management is pushing through double-digit price increases to recapture margin. Our bear-case 12-month floor is $192.71.
How Qualcomm Compares to Broadcom and Marvell
Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) is the aspirational benchmark. Broadcom’s Q3 FY26 AI semiconductor revenue hit $16.7 billion, growing 221% year over year, with Q4 AI silicon guided to $21.7 billion.
At a $1.67 trillion market cap versus Qualcomm’s roughly $207 billion, AVGO shows what the market pays for proven hyperscaler exposure. Qualcomm’s data center revenue is aiming for a fraction of that, which is why our target treats the ramp cautiously.
Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) is the closer analog. Marvell’s Q2 FY27 data center revenue reached $2.17 billion, up 46% year over year and 79% of total revenue, with a Google custom silicon partnership tied to a warrant for up to 7% of Marvell shares.
Marvell trades at a $226 billion market cap on far less revenue than Qualcomm, which makes our $228.68 target look conservative if Qualcomm’s hyperscaler wins scale similarly.
Data Center Optionality Anchors the Thesis
Our 24/7 Wall St. price target of $228.68 reflects a buy with 90% confidence.
The tipping factor is the non-handset inflection: management is telling us fiscal 2027 growth exceeds 60% off a diversified base, and the market is still pricing Qualcomm like a handset company.
The same data center buildout powering that inflection is lifting a broader set of suppliers, seven of which we profiled in a free report on the AI infrastructure trade here: 7 Stocks Powering the AI Boom. Watch for December-quarter guidance to confirm the hyperscaler ramp and pricing actions to stabilize QCT gross margin.
These projections assume Qualcomm executes on its $40 billion non-handset target and hyperscaler custom silicon scales as guided. Upside or downside could result from Apple share loss, US-China trade actions, or HBC adoption pace after mid-2027.

Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.

A $60 Billion Amazon Opportunity Is Changing Qualcomm's Chip Story
Wed, September 30, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT 4 min read
A photo of a corporate Qualcomm sign by JHVEPhoto via Adobe Stock
Qualcomm's (QCOM) story has been under pressure. Smartphones still drive a large part of its business. However, handset revenue has weakened recently, with Apple reducing its reliance on Qualcomm for modem chips.
Now Amazon (AMZN) is giving Qualcomm something it has been chasing for years—a foothold in the AI data center market. Will this potential $60 billion deal turn Qualcomm from a smartphone chip heavyweight into a serious AI infrastructure player?
Warren Buffett Says America Is Doing Something 'Unsustainable' and Doesn't Know If We Have 2 Years or 20 —'This Can't Go On Forever'
'It's Your Only Option' — Late Billionaire Charlie Munger, 99, Shared His Iron Rule for Overcoming Life's Hardship. 'Everybody Struggles, But You Can't Quit'
Rocket Lab Steps In Where SpaceX Just Walked Away
Tired of missing midday reversals? The FREE Barchart Brief newsletter keeps you in the know. Sign up now!
Let's find out.
Sitting with a market cap of $212 billion, Qualcomm is a semiconductor and technology company best known for designing chips and licensing wireless technology. Its QCT (Qualcomm CDMA Technologies) segment is its chip business for handsets, automotive, IoT, and data centers. Meanwhile, its QTL (Qualcomm Technology Licensing) licenses its extensive portfolio of wireless technology patents to generate royalty revenue.
For years, Qualcomm's story has largely revolved around smartphones. While the smartphone business remains enormous, it has been a drag on its financials. In the fiscal third quarter, handset revenue fell 20% year-over-year (YoY) to $5.09 billion. Although automotive revenue jumped 61% and IoT revenue increased 9%, overall QCT segment revenue dipped 5% to $8.5 billion. At its June 2026 Investor Day, Qualcomm said it expects non-handset revenue to reach $40 billion by fiscal 2029, roughly twice the target it had previously established. Data centers are supposed to become a major part of that expansion, with Qualcomm targeting more than $15 billion in data center revenue by fiscal 2029.
Amazon is Opening New Doors of Opportunity
The Amazon deal opened new doors for its data center ambition. Recently, Qualcomm and Amazon announced working together on chips and other technology for Amazon's AI data centers. The partnership will initially focus on AI inference, which is the computing needed to run AI models and generate responses. Furthermore, Qualcomm will also provide the technology for moving data around these data centers at very high speeds. The agreement includes optical connectivity products based on its SerDes and optical DSP technologies, with the initial generation reaching 1.6T and later generations planned.
This is where Qualcomm's $2.4 billion acquisition of Alphawave will be beneficial. It allows Qualcomm to use a broader portfolio in an actual hyperscale deployment. In other words, this partnership is expected to cover several generations of products, so this is bigger than a one-time chip order.
As part of the agreement, Amazon received the right to buy up to 25 million Qualcomm shares at $161.26 per share. Some of those rights become available as Amazon meets certain commitments to buy Qualcomm's data center products and services. Those purchases can eventually reach as much as $60 billion under the agreement. However, this doesn't mean that Amazon has agreed to outright pay Qualcomm $60 billion. It represents the maximum level of purchases tied to the agreement's warrant structure.
The timing of this deal is just perfect for Qualcomm's data center buildout. After the Amazon agreement, CFO Palkhiwala is now highly confident of achieving the data center target, as Qualcomm already has purchase orders and is producing chips for Amazon. The company expects revenue from Amazon to begin in the December quarter. Palkhiwala also specifically said that while Amazon is one of the core components supporting the company's fiscal 2029 goal, the company is also working with another undisclosed hyperscaler.
Amazon Could Be the Proof Qualcomm Needed
Qualcomm has spent years trying to prove that its expertise in low-power computing, connectivity, and chip design can take the company beyond smartphones. While Automotive and IoT have already proved that, Amazon now gives Qualcomm a hyperscale customer and a real opportunity to establish itself in AI infrastructure. For Qualcomm, the Amazon deal may just be the validation it needed. It gives the company a foothold in a market where spending is surging and where Qualcomm has been trying to build a business.
That said, Qualcomm still has to turn Amazon's commitment into large-scale deployments and prove that its chips can deliver the performance, power efficiency, and reliability that hyperscalers demand.
On Wall Street, QCOM stock holds a consensus "Hold" rating. Of the 33 analysts covering the stock, nine rate it a "Strong Buy," two say it is a "Moderate Buy," 18 recommend holding it, while one says it is a "Moderate Sell," and three rate it a "Strong Sell." QCOM has climbed 9% year-to-date (YTD) and currently trades just below its mean target price of $198.31. However, its high target price of $400 implies an upside potential of 114% over the next year.

judge_card:
Company: QCOM
Jan research (many sources; citations and numbers checked by code against each source):
- Micron Technology signed long-term supply agreements with GM and Ford for automotive memory and started construction of a New York semiconductor fab. [https://www.fool.com/coverage/charts/2026/10/04/micron-technology-vs-qualcomm-what-revenue-trends-tell-investors-about-these-tech-companies/] (2026-10-04)
- Qualcomm's CFO stated that Snapdragon platforms for agentic AI are designed for high-end smartphones with best-in-class gaming and productivity performance. [https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/agentic-ai-power-qualcomm-qcom-011118232.html] (2026-10-04)
- The Motley Fool's Stock Advisor did not recommend Micron Technology as one of their top 10 stocks to buy. [https://www.aol.com/articles/micron-technology-vs-qualcomm-revenue-054012000.html] (2026-10-04)
- Qualcomm renewed a global patent license agreement with Apple for royalty payments through 2027. [https://www.fool.com/coverage/charts/2026/10/03/asml-holding-vs-qualcomm-what-revenue-trends-tell-investors-about-these-semiconductor-industry-giants/] (2026-10-03)
- Qualcomm extended its licensing agreement with Apple starting April 1, 2027, after the current agreement expired on that date. [https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/01/qualcomm-just-inked-a-surprise-apple-deal-and-announced-the-future-of-personal-ai/] (2026-10-01)
- Qualcomm's new silicon enables AI processing on smartphones, glasses, and earbuds, as demonstrated in smart glasses with Mastercard integration. [https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/01/qualcomm-just-inked-a-surprise-apple-deal-and-announced-the-future-of-personal-ai/] (2026-10-01)
- The Qualcomm-Apple licensing deal is expected to generate $1.5 billion to $1.7 billion in annual revenue, or $7.50 per phone. [https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/01/qualcomm-just-inked-a-surprise-apple-deal-and-announced-the-future-of-personal-ai/] (2026-10-01)
- Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon described the 'agentic age' where users collaborate with AI technology rather than interact with tools. [https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/01/qualcomm-just-inked-a-surprise-apple-deal-and-announced-the-future-of-personal-ai/] (2026-10-01)
- Qualcomm's AI agents can scan environments, hear users, and process requests natively on devices like smart glasses. [https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/01/qualcomm-just-inked-a-surprise-apple-deal-and-announced-the-future-of-personal-ai/] (2026-10-01)
- Apple previously attempted to reduce reliance on Qualcomm by developing its own modems, spending over six years building its own chip. [https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/01/qualcomm-just-inked-a-surprise-apple-deal-and-announced-the-future-of-personal-ai/] (2026-10-01)
- Analyst Stacy Rasgon from Bernstein expects more details about the Qualcomm-Apple deal during Qualcomm's next earnings call on Nov. 4. [https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/01/qualcomm-just-inked-a-surprise-apple-deal-and-announced-the-future-of-personal-ai/] (2026-10-01)
- Qualcomm's market cap is $184.04 billion with a 52-week trading range of $121.99 to $259.92 as of September 30, 2026. [https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/qualcomm-qcom-ai-strategy-overcome-180128531.html] (2026-09-30)
- Qualcomm targets more than $15 billion in data center revenue by fiscal 2029, with Amazon partnership expected to cover up to $60 billion in purchases. [https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/60-billion-amazon-opportunity-changing-113002913.html] (2026-09-30)
- Amazon received the right to buy up to 25 million Qualcomm shares at $161.26 per share under the partnership agreement. [https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/60-billion-amazon-opportunity-changing-113002913.html] (2026-09-30)
- Qualcomm's QTL segment licenses wireless technology patents to generate royalty revenue. [https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/60-billion-amazon-opportunity-changing-113002913.html] (2026-09-30)

As the artificial intelligence boom matures, choosing between high-growth processors and steady analog chips requires a careful look at Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +2.95%) and Texas Instruments (TXN +4.44%) as potential long-term investments.
Advanced Micro Devices focuses on high-performance computing for data centers and gaming, while Texas Instruments dominates the analog world with chips for industrial and automotive uses. While both operate in the same broad category, their business models and growth profiles offer very different opportunities for retail investors today.
Advanced Micro Devices designs processors and graphics chips for everything from laptops to massive data centers. Key partnerships include a strategic agreement with OpenAI to deploy advanced graphics units, alongside long-term deals with Sony (SONY +1.41%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) for gaming hardware. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business since a few large buyers drive much of the volume.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $34.6 billion, an increase of 34% over the prior year. Net income was roughly $4.3 billion, and AMD reported a net margin of approximately 12.5% for the year. This upward trend highlights the strong demand for the company's newest products among semiconductor stocks.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1, indicating that AMD relies very little on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to pay short-term debts with current assets, is roughly 2.9. Free cash flow reached nearly $6.7 billion, though note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 21.2% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Texas Instruments offers a massive catalog of more than 80,000 products, focusing on analog and embedded processing. The company serves over 100,000 customers globally, primarily in the industrial and automotive markets. Because the customer base is highly diverse, with roughly half of total revenue generated by customers outside of its largest 50, the company does not rely heavily on any single buyer.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $17.7 billion, up 13% compared to the previous year. Net income was $5 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 28%. In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, Texas Instruments highlighted its focus on making electronics more affordable through its manufacturing scale.
Based on the December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is close to 0.9. The current ratio is approximately 4.4, suggesting the company maintains a strong cushion for its immediate financial obligations. Free cash flow for the year was nearly $2.6 billion, providing capital to support its long-term manufacturing expansion and return value to shareholders.
Advanced Micro Devices faces intense competition from Intel (INTC -0.56%) and Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%), especially following strategic partnerships between those rivals. Geopolitical risks are also present, as U.S. export controls on advanced chips to China have caused inventory charges. Additionally, the company relies heavily on TSMC (TSM +2.96%) for manufacturing and must navigate the integration of recent acquisitions like ZT Systems.
Texas Instruments must manage the cyclical nature of the chip industry, which often sees volatile demand. Because the company owns its manufacturing plants, it faces high fixed costs that are difficult to reduce during market downturns. Significant revenue comes from customers in China, making it vulnerable to trade barriers. TI is also currently in the middle of acquiring Silicon Laboratories (SLAB +0.11%).
Advanced Micro Devices trades at a significantly higher premium than Texas Instruments when comparing the forward P/E and P/S ratio metrics.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Presumably, investors are paying a premium for AMD because of its strong revenue growth (Texas Instruments' growth didn't come close to AMD's last fiscal year). That said, I am more interested in each company's net margin. Using fiscal 2025 figures, TI's margin pretty handily tops AMD's full-year results. And while both companies have seen profits expand by a few percentage points over the trailing 12 months, that profitability gap has continued into this fiscal year.
As far as their actual business models, I do think AMD's fabless approach is more attractive, because it gives the company more flexibility. Texas Instruments, conversely, has to deal with the high fixed costs of owning and running its manufacturing plants.
AMD stock has absolutely exploded over the past 10 years, while Texas Instruments shares have modestly outperformed the S&P 500 over that same time frame. Past performance is no indication of future results, but it's worth taking into consideration.
All told, I like Texas Instruments better here because it appeals to the conservative side of me: It’s not crazy expensive, it has stronger profitability, and it pays a dividend yielding just over 2.1%.

Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) stock is up 55% year to date and trades at $264.70, a rally that's beaten the broad market by a wide margin while still lagging its own chip sector. Meanwhile, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) is up 66% year to date, and Texas Instruments still trailed a fund weighted toward the artificial intelligence (AI) compute names, which is why a year this strong hasn't drawn the attention it deserves.
Texas Instruments stock is down 1% Monday afternoon, holding up better than the semiconductor fund's 5% decline. That's a telling single-session contrast on a day the sector's being sold hard, and it reinforces the case that Texas Instruments offers a different flavor of exposure than the AI-heavy names driving the index higher.

Analog Cycle Turned Broader Than Expected
CEO Haviv Ilan told analysts that Texas Instruments delivered revenue up 23% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, with the analog segment growing 26% and embedded processing also expanding. Pricing is the underappreciated lever for Texas Instruments. Analog chip prices typically decline a couple of points a year, yet management said prices held flat across the first half of 2026, and Texas Instruments has begun rolling out customer-by-customer price increases that started landing in the third quarter of 2026. Capacity built during the downturn also gave Texas Instruments clean-room space and inventory on hand at Richardson, Sherman and Lehigh, at a moment when rival suppliers were quoting far longer lead times.

Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI) stock is up 35% year to date, a strong run that still lands well behind Texas Instruments. Additionally, Microchip Technology (NASDAQ:MCHP) stock is up 15% year to date, the widest gap of the three. Microchip Technology has been climbing out of a deep inventory correction, and the fact that Texas Instruments installed clean-room capacity ahead of the upturn is the most plausible reason it captured share while its peer was still normalizing.
The through-line for Texas Instruments is that in analog, the constraint during an upturn is usually the ability to supply rather than the ability to sell. Texas Instruments spent the last downturn equipping the fabs its rivals now need, and that head start shows up plainly in the year-to-date scoreboard.

The bear case for Texas Instruments is that an analog upcycle remains a cycle, and a stock that's added more than half its value in under a year has already priced a fair stretch of it. MCHP Expands Ethernet Portfolio: Can it Challenge TXN & ADI?
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 6:20 AM PDT 4 min read
Microchip Technology MCHP has expanded its 10BASE-T1S Single Pair Ethernet portfolio with the launch of the LAN8679 and LAN8680 PMD transceivers and the LAN8660X/1X/2X endpoint family with integrated transceivers. The products are designed for next-generation zonal architectures across automotive, industrial, robotics and aerospace and defense applications, extending Ethernet connectivity to edge nodes while reducing wiring and system complexity. The portfolio combines transceivers, endpoint functionality, power management and embedded-control capabilities, thereby supporting MCHP's broader Total System Solutions strategy. It also improves competitive prowess against the likes of Texas Instruments TXN and Analog Devices ADI.
The LAN8679 features an Open Alliance 3-Pin interface in a compact package, while the LAN8680 adds power management, wake as well as sleep control and watchdog supervision. The LAN8660X/1X/2X family integrates a transceiver into a single-chip Remote Control Protocol solution, eliminating the need for external PHY components in applications such as control systems, lighting and audio. Microchip's 10BASE-T1S multidrop architecture can connect eight or more nodes over a single bus, helping reduce wiring weight, costs and gateway requirements.
The portfolio expansion strengthens Microchip's connectivity and networking growth strategy. The company identifies connectivity/networking as one of its new strategic growth pillars, targeting opportunities across Industry 4.0, automotive and data-center applications. MCHP highlights Single Pair Ethernet as a roughly $4-billion served available market, spanning automotive, aerospace, robotics, industrial vehicles, building controls, industrial controls, sensors, actuators and vehicle networking. The company also sees billions of legacy nodes as potential replacement opportunities, giving the expanded portfolio a sizable long-term addressable market.
The launch is also well timed with improving demand in MCHP's two largest target markets for these products. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, industrial represented 32.2% of revenues and automotive accounted for 15%. Industrial revenues increased 24.3% year over year, while automotive revenues jumped 29.3%. Industrial and automotive customers had largely completed inventory corrections, and Microchip noted that clients were placing a higher number of orders, while bookings remained strong across product lines, business units and geographies. The new devices are expected to help Microchip capture more semiconductor content as automotive and industrial networks migrate from fragmented legacy architectures toward consolidated Ethernet-based systems.
Texas Instruments' DP83TD555 targets 10BASE-T1S connectivity, while ADI's AD3300/AD3301 family brings integrated Ethernet connectivity to edge sensors and actuators.
Texas Instruments is challenging Microchip across automotive and industrial connectivity through its broad Analog and Embedded Processing portfolio, strong manufacturing capacity and growing semiconductor content per system. In the second quarter of 2026, TXN's industrial revenues increased roughly 30% year over year, while automotive revenues rose in the mid-teens. Texas Instruments' supply capabilities further intensify the challenge. The company has available clean-room space and is expanding production capacity to address rising demand.

Texas Instruments Extends Dividend Growth Streak to 23 Years with 7% Raise
Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) has raised its quarterly dividend by 7% to $1.52 per share from $1.42, bringing the annualized payout to $6.08. The increase marks the company's 23rd consecutive year of dividend growth. The new dividend is scheduled to be paid on November 10, 2026, to shareholders of record as of October 30, subject to formal board approval.
The increase is notable because TI is raising its payout while its cash generation has improved. For the 12 months through June 2026, TI generated $8.7 billion in operating cash flow and $6.5 billion in free cash flow, while returning $5.8 billion to shareholders.

Texas Instruments Extends Dividend Growth Streak to 23 Years With 7% Raise
TI's Improving Free Cash Flow Creates More Room for Dividend Growth
The 7% increase is a stronger signal for income investors than the previous 4% raise. TI is increasing the payout while its cash generation has improved sharply. In the 12 months through June 2026, the company generated $8.67 billion in operating cash flow and $6.53 billion in free cash flow, up from $1.76 billion of free cash flow a year earlier.
That improvement matters because Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) has been investing heavily in manufacturing capacity. Capital expenditures were $3.31 billion over the latest 12 months, down from $4.94 billion a year earlier. TI expects 2026 capital spending of $2 billion to $3 billion, suggesting the pressure from its elevated investment cycle is easing. The dividend also appears increasingly supported by free cash flow. TI paid $5.11 billion in dividends over the latest 12 months against $6.53 billion of free cash flow. That leaves a meaningful cushion, rather than requiring the company to fund the dividend primarily through borrowing or asset sales.
The 23-year record adds another layer of confidence. TI says its objective is to provide a dividend that is both sustainable and growing, and the latest increase is consistent with its stated goal of returning all free cash flow to owners over time.
Dividend Faces a Test From Its Investment Cycle
The main concern is that the dividend still consumes a large portion of free cash flow. Although the latest figures are much better, dividends of $5.11 billion compared with $6.53 billion of free cash flow leave less flexibility than the headline cash-flow growth might suggest. TI also continues to invest billions of dollars in manufacturing capacity.
The dividend yield is another consideration. The new $6.08 annualized payout translates to roughly a 2.3% yield at recent share prices, so investors are relying on continued dividend growth rather than a high current income stream.
There is also a risk that the recent improvement in free cash flow could moderate if TI's capital spending remains elevated or rises again with its expansion plans. The company says capital expenditures beyond 2026 will depend on revenue and growth expectations, so the cash available for dividends could remain sensitive to its investment cycle.
The 7% dividend increase makes the dividend case stronger than the earlier 4% increase suggested. Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) is now growing the payout at a healthier rate while free cash flow has recovered substantially and capital spending is coming down from its peak.
The key number to watch is the relationship between free cash flow and dividends. At present, TI is generating enough free cash flow to cover the dividend with a cushion, but the payout is still consuming a significant share of that cash. For dividend investors, the next question is whether TI can sustain its improving free cash flow trend as its manufacturing investments continue.

As the artificial intelligence boom matures, choosing between high-growth processors and steady analog chips requires a careful look at Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +2.95%) and Texas Instruments (TXN +4.44%) as potential long-term investments.
Advanced Micro Devices focuses on high-performance computing for data centers and gaming, while Texas Instruments dominates the analog world with chips for industrial and automotive uses. While both operate in the same broad category, their business models and growth profiles offer very different opportunities for retail investors today.
Advanced Micro Devices designs processors and graphics chips for everything from laptops to massive data centers. Key partnerships include a strategic agreement with OpenAI to deploy advanced graphics units, alongside long-term deals with Sony (SONY +1.41%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) for gaming hardware. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business since a few large buyers drive much of the volume.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $34.6 billion, an increase of 34% over the prior year. Net income was roughly $4.3 billion, and AMD reported a net margin of approximately 12.5% for the year. This upward trend highlights the strong demand for the company's newest products among semiconductor stocks.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1, indicating that AMD relies very little on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to pay short-term debts with current assets, is roughly 2.9. Free cash flow reached nearly $6.7 billion, though note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 21.2% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Texas Instruments offers a massive catalog of more than 80,000 products, focusing on analog and embedded processing. The company serves over 100,000 customers globally, primarily in the industrial and automotive markets. Because the customer base is highly diverse, with roughly half of total revenue generated by customers outside of its largest 50, the company does not rely heavily on any single buyer.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $17.7 billion, up 13% compared to the previous year. Net income was $5 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 28%. In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, Texas Instruments highlighted its focus on making electronics more affordable through its manufacturing scale.
Based on the December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is close to 0.9. The current ratio is approximately 4.4, suggesting the company maintains a strong cushion for its immediate financial obligations. Free cash flow for the year was nearly $2.6 billion, providing capital to support its long-term manufacturing expansion and return value to shareholders.
Advanced Micro Devices faces intense competition from Intel (INTC -0.56%) and Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%), especially following strategic partnerships between those rivals. Geopolitical risks are also present, as U.S. export controls on advanced chips to China have caused inventory charges. Additionally, the company relies heavily on TSMC (TSM +2.96%) for manufacturing and must navigate the integration of recent acquisitions like ZT Systems.
Texas Instruments must manage the cyclical nature of the chip industry, which often sees volatile demand. Because the company owns its manufacturing plants, it faces high fixed costs that are difficult to reduce during market downturns. Significant revenue comes from customers in China, making it vulnerable to trade barriers. TI is also currently in the middle of acquiring Silicon Laboratories (SLAB +0.11%).
Advanced Micro Devices trades at a significantly higher premium than Texas Instruments when comparing the forward P/E and P/S ratio metrics.
MetricAdvanced Micro DevicesTexas Instruments

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Presumably, investors are paying a premium for AMD because of its strong revenue growth (Texas Instruments' growth didn't come close to AMD's last fiscal year). That said, I am more interested in each company's net margin. Using fiscal 2025 figures, TI's margin pretty handily tops AMD's full-year results. And while both companies have seen profits expand by a few percentage points over the trailing 12 months, that profitability gap has continued into this fiscal year.
As far as their actual business models, I do think AMD's fabless approach is more attractive, because it gives the company more flexibility. Texas Instruments, conversely, has to deal with the high fixed costs of owning and running its manufacturing plants.
AMD stock has absolutely exploded over the past 10 years, while Texas Instruments shares have modestly outperformed the S&P 500 over that same time frame. Past performance is no indication of future results, but it's worth taking into consideration.
All told, I like Texas Instruments better here because it appeals to the conservative side of me: It’s not crazy expensive, it has stronger profitability, and it pays a dividend yielding just over 2.1%.

Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN) stock is up 55% year to date and trades at $264.70, a rally that's beaten the broad market by a wide margin while still lagging its own chip sector. The gain puts Texas Instruments among the year's strongest large-cap analog winners, even after a soft Monday session in the semiconductor group.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 12% year to date, so Texas Instruments has cleared the broad tape by roughly a factor of five. Meanwhile, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) is up 66% year to date, and Texas Instruments still trailed a fund weighted toward the artificial intelligence (AI) compute names, which is why a year this strong hasn't drawn the attention it deserves.
Texas Instruments stock is down 1% Monday afternoon, holding up better than the semiconductor fund's 5% decline. That's a telling single-session contrast on a day the sector's being sold hard, and it reinforces the case that Texas Instruments offers a different flavor of exposure than the AI-heavy names driving the index higher.

Analog Cycle Turned Broader Than Expected
CEO Haviv Ilan told analysts that Texas Instruments delivered revenue up 23% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, with the analog segment growing 26% and embedded processing also expanding. Ilan said industrial demand at Texas Instruments climbed 30% year over year, with growth broad across every sector and every region.

Data center revenue at Texas Instruments doubled year over year, and automotive rose at a mid-teens pace, accelerated by electric and hybrid demand in China and by customers running their own inventories to unsustainably low levels. Ilan framed the setup on the earnings call: "I think we are in the start of a cycle that is very, very broad."
TXN Earnings Explorer — 24/7 Wall St.
Pricing is the underappreciated lever for Texas Instruments. Analog chip prices typically decline a couple of points a year, yet management said prices held flat across the first half of 2026, and Texas Instruments has begun rolling out customer-by-customer price increases that started landing in the third quarter of 2026. Capacity built during the downturn also gave Texas Instruments clean-room space and inventory on hand at Richardson, Sherman and Lehigh, at a moment when rival suppliers were quoting far longer lead times.
Texas Instruments also received $850 million in CHIPS Act incentives during the second quarter, adding to a free cash flow rebuild that underpins its shareholder returns. Trailing free cash flow at Texas Instruments reached $6.5 billion, and the company returned $5.8 billion to owners over the same window.
Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI) stock is up 35% year to date, a strong run that still lands well behind Texas Instruments. Analog Devices rode the same industrial and communications tailwind, yet Texas Instruments converted that demand into more revenue and did so with a manufacturing footprint already sized for the recovery.
Additionally, Microchip Technology (NASDAQ:MCHP) stock is up 15% year to date, the widest gap of the three. Microchip Technology has been climbing out of a deep inventory correction, and the fact that Texas Instruments installed clean-room capacity ahead of the upturn is the most plausible reason it captured share while its peer was still normalizing.
The through-line for Texas Instruments is that in analog, the constraint during an upturn is usually the ability to supply rather than the ability to sell. Texas Instruments spent the last downturn equipping the fabs its rivals now need, and that head start shows up plainly in the year-to-date scoreboard.
Texas Instruments guided third-quarter revenue to $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and EPS to $2.23 to $2.57, a range that would extend the sequential and year-over-year growth pattern. The bull case for Texas Instruments rests on Ilan's view that the cycle is early and unusually broad, with industrial, data center and automotive contributing at once, and with pricing rising in a business where it normally erodes.

The bear case for Texas Instruments is that an analog upcycle remains a cycle, and a stock that's added more than half its value in under a year has already priced a fair stretch of it. Trailing its own semiconductor fund is both why Texas Instruments reads as an overlooked story (the kind we cataloged in a free report on the winners most investors walked past) and why the market may prefer the chips that train models to the ones powering the racks around them.
Investors weighing fresh exposure to Texas Instruments may want to keep an eye on whether the third-quarter pricing actions hold, and size their positions with that duality in mind. Zephyr Project Expands Semiconductor Industry Support as Texas Instruments and Infineon Technologies Upgrade to Platinum Membership
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 7:00 AM PDT 4 min read
Texas Instruments and Infineon Technologies have upgraded to Platinum membership in the Zephyr Project, deepening their investment in the open source RTOS and its developer community.
These increased commitments provide additional resources for Zephyr's technical development, infrastructure and community programs.
The announcement coincides with the Zephyr Developer Summit (Oct. 7-9) and Zephyr Maintainers Forum (Oct. 6) in Prague, where the community marks Zephyr's 10th anniversary with more than 40 technical sessions, over 45 speakers and the first-ever Zephyr Community Awards.
PRAGUE, Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Zephyr Developer Summit – The Zephyr® Project, an open source project at the Linux Foundation building a secure, connected and flexible real-time operating system (RTOS) for resource-constrained devices, today announced that Texas Instruments (TI) and Infineon Technologies have upgraded to Platinum membership. Announced ahead of the Zephyr Developer Summit, co-located with Open Source Summit Europe, the expanded commitments from two leading semiconductor companies reinforce growing industry investment in Zephyr as a vendor-neutral, open source foundation for embedded development.
TI and Infineon bring longstanding technical relationships with the Zephyr community. TI has contributed to the project since its inception in 2016, providing software and board support while integrating Zephyr across its embedded portfolio. Infineon is also an active contributor and supports Zephyr across multiple embedded platforms. The move to Platinum membership will provide additional resources for the project's technical development, infrastructure and community programs.
"Ten years ago, Zephyr set out to give the embedded industry a common open source RTOS that companies could build on together," said Kate Stewart, Vice President of Dependable Embedded Systems at the Linux Foundation. "Seeing two major semiconductor companies that have contributed to Zephyr for years increase their participation is a strong sign of how far that model has come. This support gives the community more resources and makes Zephyr available to more developers building embedded products."
Since its launch, Zephyr has grown into a global ecosystem spanning a broad range of architectures, boards and embedded applications. As open source plays a growing role in embedded development, Zephyr provides a common platform where semiconductor companies, developers and product manufacturers can collaborate on shared technology. The increased engagement from TI and Infineon will help Zephyr advance its technology, hardware ecosystem and developer community as it enters its second decade.
"As a platinum-level member, Infineon is expanding its investment in the Zephyr community to help developers bring connected, resource-constrained devices to market more efficiently," said Clark Jarvis, Zephyr Governing Board Representative at Infineon. "Building on a decade of Zephyr innovation, we are committed to enabling greater software reuse and portability across our microcontroller (MCU), automotive MCU, and connectivity portfolios. This deeper engagement reflects our ambition to deliver an even better developer experience, strengthen security, and broaden hardware support throughout the Zephyr ecosystem."
"TI is committed to breaking down the barriers between hardware and software through continuous innovation. The Zephyr Project is a cornerstone of that effort," said Marian Kost, vice president and general manager of Wireless Connectivity at TI. "We are continuing our investment in open-source software and the developer community. TI wants to ensure that everyone – from a hobbyist to an engineer – can accelerate their path from concept to commercial product."
The upgraded memberships come as the Zephyr community gathers in Prague at Open Source Summit Europe to continue celebrating the project's tenth anniversary. The week opens with the Zephyr Maintainers Forum on Oct. 6, a working session where maintainers, Technical Steering Committee members and subsystem owners set the project's technical direction on release planning, security and safety support, and cross-subsystem coordination. It is followed by the Zephyr Developer Summit on Oct. 7-9, featuring more than 40 technical sessions from over 45 speakers across functional safety, security and CRA readiness, connectivity, developer tooling and testing, and real-world use cases in automotive, space and industrial applications. The summit also hosts the Zephyr Community Awards on Oct. 7, recognizing standout contributors from across the ecosystem for their work and support over the last decade.
Check out the complete Zephyr Developer Summit schedule or to learn more about the Zephyr Project and how to participate, visit zephyrproject.org.
The Zephyr® Project is an open source, scalable real-time operating system (RTOS) supporting multiple hardware architectures. To learn more, please visit www.zephyrproject.org.
The Linux Foundation is the world's leading home for collaboration on open source software, hardware, standards, and data. Linux Foundation projects, including Linux, Kubernetes, Model Context Protocol (MCP), OpenChain, OpenSearch, OpenSSF, OpenStack, PyTorch, Ray, RISC-V, SPDX and Zephyr, provide the foundation for global infrastructure. The Linux Foundation is focused on leveraging best practices and addressing the needs of contributors, users, and solution providers to create sustainable models for open collaboration. For more information, please visit us at linuxfoundation.org.
For a list of trademarks of The Linux Foundation, please see its trademark usage page: linuxfoundation.org/trademark-usage. Linux is a registered trademark of Linus Torvalds.

MCHP Expands Ethernet Portfolio: Can it Challenge TXN & ADI?
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 6:20 AM PDT 4 min read
Microchip Technology MCHP has expanded its 10BASE-T1S Single Pair Ethernet portfolio with the launch of the LAN8679 and LAN8680 PMD transceivers and the LAN8660X/1X/2X endpoint family with integrated transceivers. The products are designed for next-generation zonal architectures across automotive, industrial, robotics and aerospace and defense applications, extending Ethernet connectivity to edge nodes while reducing wiring and system complexity. The portfolio combines transceivers, endpoint functionality, power management and embedded-control capabilities, thereby supporting MCHP's broader Total System Solutions strategy. It also improves competitive prowess against the likes of Texas Instruments TXN and Analog Devices ADI.
The LAN8679 features an Open Alliance 3-Pin interface in a compact package, while the LAN8680 adds power management, wake as well as sleep control and watchdog supervision. The LAN8660X/1X/2X family integrates a transceiver into a single-chip Remote Control Protocol solution, eliminating the need for external PHY components in applications such as control systems, lighting and audio. Microchip's 10BASE-T1S multidrop architecture can connect eight or more nodes over a single bus, helping reduce wiring weight, costs and gateway requirements.
The portfolio expansion strengthens Microchip's connectivity and networking growth strategy. The company identifies connectivity/networking as one of its new strategic growth pillars, targeting opportunities across Industry 4.0, automotive and data-center applications. MCHP highlights Single Pair Ethernet as a roughly $4-billion served available market, spanning automotive, aerospace, robotics, industrial vehicles, building controls, industrial controls, sensors, actuators and vehicle networking. The company also sees billions of legacy nodes as potential replacement opportunities, giving the expanded portfolio a sizable long-term addressable market.
The launch is also well timed with improving demand in MCHP's two largest target markets for these products. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, industrial represented 32.2% of revenues and automotive accounted for 15%. Industrial revenues increased 24.3% year over year, while automotive revenues jumped 29.3%. Industrial and automotive customers had largely completed inventory corrections, and Microchip noted that clients were placing a higher number of orders, while bookings remained strong across product lines, business units and geographies. The new devices are expected to help Microchip capture more semiconductor content as automotive and industrial networks migrate from fragmented legacy architectures toward consolidated Ethernet-based systems.
Texas Instruments' DP83TD555 targets 10BASE-T1S connectivity, while ADI's AD3300/AD3301 family brings integrated Ethernet connectivity to edge sensors and actuators.
Texas Instruments is challenging Microchip across automotive and industrial connectivity through its broad Analog and Embedded Processing portfolio, strong manufacturing capacity and growing semiconductor content per system. In the second quarter of 2026, TXN's industrial revenues increased roughly 30% year over year, while automotive revenues rose in the mid-teens. Texas Instruments' supply capabilities further intensify the challenge. The company has available clean-room space and is expanding production capacity to address rising demand.
Analog Devices poses a significant challenge through its high-performance analog, sensing, power and embedded technologies. Industrial accounted for 49% of ADI's third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenues and increased 53% year over year, led partly by automation, while automotive represented 25% of revenues and grew 16%. ADI said its higher content and share positions are driving automotive growth across next-generation ADAS, infotainment and electric powertrains. ADI is also positioning for the emergence of physical AI, including robotics and autonomous mobility.
MCHP's Share Price Performance, Valuation & Estimates
Shares of Microchip have appreciated 22% year to date, outperforming the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector's rise of 21.8%.
The MCHP stock is trading at a premium, with a trailing price/book multiple of 6.55 compared with the Zacks Semiconductor – Analog and Mixed industry's 6.48. Microchip has a Value Score of D.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Microchip's fiscal 2027 earnings is currently pegged at $3.63 per share, up 15.6% over the past 30 days, suggesting 121.3% growth from fiscal 2026's reported figure.

Texas Instruments Extends Dividend Growth Streak to 23 Years with 7% Raise
Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) has raised its quarterly dividend by 7% to $1.52 per share from $1.42, bringing the annualized payout to $6.08. The increase marks the company's 23rd consecutive year of dividend growth. The new dividend is scheduled to be paid on November 10, 2026, to shareholders of record as of October 30, subject to formal board approval.
The increase is notable because TI is raising its payout while its cash generation has improved. For the 12 months through June 2026, TI generated $8.7 billion in operating cash flow and $6.5 billion in free cash flow, while returning $5.8 billion to shareholders.
Also read: McDonald's (MCD) Achieves 'Dividend King' Status as It Raises Payout for 50 Consecutive Years
Texas Instruments Extends Dividend Growth Streak to 23 Years With 7% Raise
TI's Improving Free Cash Flow Creates More Room for Dividend Growth
The 7% increase is a stronger signal for income investors than the previous 4% raise. TI is increasing the payout while its cash generation has improved sharply. In the 12 months through June 2026, the company generated $8.67 billion in operating cash flow and $6.53 billion in free cash flow, up from $1.76 billion of free cash flow a year earlier.
That improvement matters because Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) has been investing heavily in manufacturing capacity. Capital expenditures were $3.31 billion over the latest 12 months, down from $4.94 billion a year earlier. TI expects 2026 capital spending of $2 billion to $3 billion, suggesting the pressure from its elevated investment cycle is easing. The dividend also appears increasingly supported by free cash flow. TI paid $5.11 billion in dividends over the latest 12 months against $6.53 billion of free cash flow. That leaves a meaningful cushion, rather than requiring the company to fund the dividend primarily through borrowing or asset sales.
The 23-year record adds another layer of confidence. TI says its objective is to provide a dividend that is both sustainable and growing, and the latest increase is consistent with its stated goal of returning all free cash flow to owners over time.
Dividend Faces a Test From Its Investment Cycle
The main concern is that the dividend still consumes a large portion of free cash flow. Although the latest figures are much better, dividends of $5.11 billion compared with $6.53 billion of free cash flow leave less flexibility than the headline cash-flow growth might suggest. TI also continues to invest billions of dollars in manufacturing capacity.
The dividend yield is another consideration. The new $6.08 annualized payout translates to roughly a 2.3% yield at recent share prices, so investors are relying on continued dividend growth rather than a high current income stream.
There is also a risk that the recent improvement in free cash flow could moderate if TI's capital spending remains elevated or rises again with its expansion plans. The company says capital expenditures beyond 2026 will depend on revenue and growth expectations, so the cash available for dividends could remain sensitive to its investment cycle.
The 7% dividend increase makes the dividend case stronger than the earlier 4% increase suggested. Texas Instruments Incorporated (NASDAQ:TXN) is now growing the payout at a healthier rate while free cash flow has recovered substantially and capital spending is coming down from its peak.
The key number to watch is the relationship between free cash flow and dividends. At present, TI is generating enough free cash flow to cover the dividend with a cushion, but the payout is still consuming a significant share of that cash. For dividend investors, the next question is whether TI can sustain its improving free cash flow trend as its manufacturing investments continue.

Texas Instruments (TXN) Soars 3.3%: Is Further Upside Left in the Stock?
Texas Instruments TXN shares rallied 3.3% in the last trading session to close at $266.64. This move can be attributable to notable volume with a higher number of shares being traded than in a typical session. This compares to the stock's 2.8% loss over the past four weeks.
The optimism surrounding the stock can be attributed to Texas Instruments raising its quarterly dividend by 7% to $1.52 per share, marking its 23rd consecutive year of dividend increases. Further, strong demand across industrial, automotive and data center markets is supporting the company's growth prospects, with second-quarter revenue rising 23% year over year, while data center revenue doubled and industrial revenue increased around 30%.
This chipmaker is expected to post quarterly earnings of $2.39 per share in its upcoming report, which represents a year-over-year change of +61.5%. Revenues are expected to be $5.91 billion, up 24.7% from the year-ago quarter.
Earnings and revenue growth expectations certainly give a good sense of the potential strength in a stock, but empirical research shows that trends in earnings estimate revisions are strongly correlated with near-term stock price movements.
For Texas Instruments, the consensus EPS estimate for the quarter has remained unchanged over the last 30 days. And a stock's price usually doesn't keep moving higher in the absence of any trend in earnings estimate revisions. So, make sure to keep an eye on TXN going forward to see if this recent jump can turn into more strength down the road.
The stock currently carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). You can see the complete list of today's Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) stocks here >>>>
Texas Instruments is a member of the Zacks Semiconductor - General industry. One other stock in the same industry, STMicroelectronics STM, finished the last trading session 3.2% higher at $50.18. STM has returned -2.6% over the past month.
For STMicroelectronics, the consensus EPS estimate for the upcoming report has remained unchanged over the past month at $0.4. This represents a change of +37.9% from what the company reported a year ago. STMicroelectronics currently has a Zacks Rank of #3 (Hold).

•"Over the past 12 months we invested $3.9 billion in R&D and SG&A, invested $3.3 billion in capital expenditures and returned $5.8 billion to owners.
•"TI's third quarter outlook is for revenue in the range of $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and earnings per share between $2.23 and $2.57."
